utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We are here to deal with a matter which has to do with case number, Mr. Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-14/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution first? Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, and Ms. Erasmus is the case manager for the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Mikulicic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Goran Mikulicic, and I represent Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski as Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We have here also a representative of the Croatian Embassy. Can you introduce yourself, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJENIC
utterances.text: My name is Orsat Miljenic. I am First Secretary of the Croatian Embassy in The Hague, and I am here, as you wished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for coming. The Chamber wanted to have this hearing because it was notified of a motion for the provisional release of Mr. Aleksovski once and now a second time, and the Chamber felt that we needed to discuss this matter in public. Therefore, I think the best way of proceeding would be to give the floor to Mr. Mikulicic, that is, the Defence; after that, to Mr. Niemann on behalf of the Prosecution; and also, we can give the floor to the representative of Croatia regarding guarantees of cooperation in addressing this issue. So let us begin with Mr. Mikulicic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning once more, Your Honours, and my learned friends from the Prosecution. As Your Honours are aware, the trial of my client, Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski, started before this Honourable Tribunal in January this year. Mr. Aleksovski was delivered to the appropriate bodies of the Tribunal last year, at the end of April. Before that, the Republic of Croatia or, rather, the Ministry of the Interior, acting upon instructions from the Tribunal, arrested Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and then the actual process of delivery to the Tribunal took place. Allow me to remind you of some facts related to these previous proceedings. When this International Tribunal was formed, the Republic of Croatia adopted a law whereby it established the basic principles for its cooperation with this Tribunal. It is a constitutional law; in other words, a law which, according to the national legislation of any country, plays a significant part in the overall structure of laws. This law obliges the Republic of Croatia to cooperate in every respect with the International Criminal Tribunal and to act according to the requests of this Tribunal as required by the bodies of the Tribunal. I don't know whether it is necessary to refer to the fact that the law on cooperation with the International Tribunal was adopted throughout the world but in a limited number of countries, so that these laws are rather the exception than the rule in the International Community of sovereign states. I wish thereby to underline the fact that from the very first moment that the Tribunal was formed, the Republic of Croatia manifested good faith to cooperate with the Tribunal. So in accordance and pursuant to the constitutional law on cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, Mr. Aleksovski was arrested on the 8th of June, 1996, and he has been in detention since then. Partly he was in the custody of the Republic of Croatia and, as of the 28th of April, 1997, he has been held in the United Nations' detention unit in The Hague. While he was in custody in the Republic of Croatia, in accordance with the law I have referred to, the procedure of giving over the accused to the International Tribunal was carried out in the District Court in Split as that was the competent court for the area in which Mr. Aleksovski was arrested. Due to reasons of health, in the course of those proceedings, Mr. Aleksovski was transferred to a specialised prison hospital in the capital of the Republic of Croatia, in Zagreb. It is the only hospital of its kind in Croatia which specialises in medical treatment of detained persons and persons serving a prison sentence. That hospital, of course, does not have any pretensions of being a high quality clinic, so that many tests and checkups have to be done in civilian hospitals under escort of prison authorities. Precisely due to these health difficulties, the Minister of Justice of the Republic of Croatia, by his decision, postponed the handover of Zlatko Aleksovski to this Tribunal because, in accordance with the laws of the Republic of Croatia, it is stipulated that if a person is suffering from any medical problems, he has to be treated first before being given over to the custody of the Tribunal. After the Defendant's health was more or less stabilised, he was handed over to the Tribunal, as I said, on the 28th of April, 1997. I am saying all this because I wish to emphasise two very important circumstances: One is that from the very first, the Republic of Croatia demonstrated absolute readiness to cooperate with the Tribunal and, secondly, that my Defendant, Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski, has certain chronic ailments about which I, as a layman, cannot say much, except by referring to the medical documentation which exists ever since the time he was held in the prison hospital in Croatia and also in the detention unit of the United Nations here in The Hague. Precisely because of his health, Your Honours, you allowed our hearings to take place during half a day only so that Mr. Aleksovski would be able to follow those proceedings. I should like to remind you of a rather unpleasant incident when Mr. Aleksovski fainted during a sitting due to the fact that physically he is unable to be immobile for long periods of time because of those ailments that I have referred to. This trial has entered its final stages. Both the Prosecution and the Defence have filed their closing statements, and it was normal to expect those final statements to be made orally, but due to various circumstances that you are familiar with, which I would not like to go into so as not to waste time, there has been a stay in the proceedings awaiting the position and ruling of the Appeals Chamber. In view of such a situation, it is not quite clear when the proceedings may be resumed, so allow me to recall the Status Conference held on the 17th of November this year when, considering the possibility of the resumption of proceedings, you realistically assessed that this may not occur before May or June next year, that is, that the trial may not be completed before then. The Defence wishes to say, by making these references, that the proceedings have been extended far beyond the date we had expected. In view of such a situation, referring to Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal, the Defence has submitted a motion for the provisional release of Mr. Aleksovski. It is our view that this Defence motion is founded on circumstances envisaged by Rule 65 itself and also it is based on certain precedents within this Tribunal. Allow me to recall some of the circumstances which the Defence considers to be important when a determination is made about this request. The Defence fully understands, in view of the significance and the seriousness of the offences that are being tried before this Chamber, that detention is the rule and provisional release the exception. However, it is in this particular case the Defence feels that this exceptional possibility of the Defendant being able to defend himself in freedom can apply. In view of the existence of exceptional circumstances that are required for provisional release of the accused, the Defence feels that such exceptional circumstances are in place. They are reflected in the fact that the Defendant has been in detention for more than two and a half years, and the Defence feels the duration of this detention is in itself an exceptional circumstance because modern European laws, in accordance with the European Commission for Human Rights, are prone to reducing that detention as much as possible in such proceedings. Allow me to tell you, Your Honours, how the Croatian law regulates this. The Croatian Penal Code does envisage detention of the accused on the basis of the view that detention is a measure to ensure the accused's presence in the proceedings. Detention is not a punitive measure; it is one of the measures which a criminal court pronounces in relation to the accused in order to ensure his presence at trial and also in order to prevent any future commission of criminal offences. These are circumstances which are decisive when a ruling is made on detention according to the laws of the Republic of Croatia, which means that detention, as a rule, is envisaged for those perpetrators of criminal offences who do not have a regular place of residence so it is not quite certain that court summons will reach them, and for those accused for whom it has been established that they have a tendency towards criminal acts so that if they were allowed to live at liberty, they may repeat such offences. So it is a measure of society to prevent such offences. Even under those circumstances, detention in the investigating stage of the proceedings may not last longer than six months. If, upon the expiry of six months, the procedure has not been completed, the accused must be released, regardless of the existence of all these circumstances I have described. So that would be, very briefly, the way in which Croatian laws deal with detention. In this specific case, the detention period, counting the time spent in the Republic of Croatia and the time in the U.N. detention centre here, has been going on for more than two and a half years. So it is far beyond any time limits which are considered, in modern legal theory, appropriate for pre-trial detention. The condition of the health of my Defendant, Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski, is of such a nature that for him to be able to function normally, it is absolutely essential that he should have freedom of movement and that he should be able, on a daily basis and particularly when his condition deteriorates, to be under the supervision and control of a physician or a physiotherapist. It is quite obvious that the conditions under which he has been living over the past two and a half years do not definitely give him the opportunity, not to improve his condition but even to maintain it at a satisfactory level from a medical standpoint. In spite of the fact that the Kingdom of the Netherlands is providing a very high standard of medical care, it is a fact that that medical care, under conditions of detention in the U.N. unit, is not applied to the extent to which in this case it would be necessary. That is the reason why the condition of Mr. Aleksovski is unstable. He suffers from vertigo, pains in the lumbar and cervical areas of the vertebral column, troubles and difficulties which require exercises; his ability to concentrate, to sleep at night, has been impaired because due to these disorders, he suffers from insomnia and has to take certain sedatives, and we all know that such sedatives do not really treat the cause of the disease but only partially treat the consequences. Years are passing, Mr. Aleksovski is getting older, and, of course, these ailments are worsening. However, the Defence firmly believes that under different conditions, if Mr. Aleksovski could be treated daily, and this treatment would consist of exercises and physiotherapy and freedom of movement in open space rather than within a limited area, would significantly improve his condition. So we are underlining these circumstances which we consider to be exceptional. Similarly, it is the view of the Defence that there is absolutely no risk that the provisional release of the accused would in any way jeopardise or impair the regular operation of this Tribunal. The Defence wishes to assure Your Honours that there is no reason at all to fear that my defendant, Mr. Aleksovski, would not respond to a court summons and appear in this courtroom or any other courtroom in which the Trial Chamber is sitting. Mr. Aleksovski is a family man who has unfortunately been separated from his family for quite some time. Like his family, he has permanent residence in the Republic of Croatia so that his release would mean that he would reside where he has permanent residence and, of course, would be prepared to a restriction of his freedom of movement. The Defence proposes that such freedom of movement could be limited by applying domestic Croatian law, and that law envisages the possibility that the competent state body, in this case, the Ministry of the Interior or the Ministry of Justice, temporarily deprive the person for whom such a measure is envisaged of his passport, thereby preventing him from leaving his place of residence in his domicile state. Another measure that is envisaged is stricter police supervision in the sense that police supervision can be provided on a 24-hour basis so that the accused could not leave his residence without reporting to the police. Something else I wish to underline is that the penal legislation of the Republic of Croatia has built-in provisions which fully comply with the high standards of this Tribunal with respect to the application of those provisions, whereby the accused can be under the obligation to respond to a summons from this Court at all times, so I think that the readiness of the Republic of Croatia to apply these measures should not be doubted at all. That readiness has been demonstrated repeatedly, and in this particular case, the readiness of the Republic of Croatia is confirmed by the very arrest of Mr. Aleksovski and the proceedings undertaken to transfer him into the custody of this Tribunal. The Defence wishes to underline the fact that measures to ensure the presence of Mr. Aleksovski at trial which are being applied, in this case, detention is not absolutely necessary in this case. It would be sufficient to apply the other measures that are at the disposal of the law, those that I have referred to, and that is, limited movement within the place of residence by temporary confiscation of the accused's passport. The passport would be deposited with the competent body, and police control would be provided on a 24-hour basis. The next requirement envisaged for the provisional release of the accused is a provision envisaged in the national law of the Republic of Croatia, and that is that the accused will not represent any threat to the victims, witnesses, or any other persons he may come into contact with. As I mentioned a moment ago, the point is to prevent the possibility of an accused being at liberty repeating an offence or constituting a threat. That simply is not possible in this case. Mr. Aleksovski is charged with criminal offences committed in the municipality of Busovaca in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in the course of these proceedings, Your Honours, you have had occasion to hear and see witnesses from the area, and you, yourself, have seen that all these people are continuing to live in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, therefore, in another state in relation to the state in which Mr. Aleksovski is domiciled. Therefore, there is simply no opportunity for him to come into contact with those people because, as I have just said, his movement, by deposition of his passport and by police supervision, would be limited. Therefore, there would be no physical possibility of Mr. Aleksovski getting into touch with those people or of him constituting any kind of threat to any witnesses, victims, or any third parties involved in these proceedings. Such a possibility is ruled out for the simple reason that those persons that Mr. Aleksovski could possibly influence are living in the territory of another state to which Mr. Aleksovski would not be able to travel because of the measures I have referred to. Regarding the last precondition, and that is the host country's opinion on this case, I have seen, Your Honours, that you have requested from the authorised bodies of the Dutch authorities their opinion on this, but I would like to remind you of the already expressed position of the Dutch authorities when they stated in brief that they will not go into court decisions, and if any of the detainees happen to be released, then the Dutch authorities would act within their national laws which say that a person who happened to be on Dutch territory, if they did not have a permit for residence on the territory of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, would simply be sent to the country from which they had been brought into the Netherlands, meaning that with the release of Mr. Aleksovski, the Dutch authorities would simply act in accordance with their regulations, and Mr. Aleksovski would be returned to the Republic of Croatia where he was originally brought from, in view of the fact that Mr. Aleksovski does not have a residence permit in the territory of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. So all of these circumstances, in the view of the Defence, point to the fact that really there is a possibility to apply Rule 65(B) on the provisional release of the accused. I would also like to ask you to take into account, without pretensions to prejudice any facts which have been presented in the proceedings, to take into account circumstances indicating any doubts that Mr. Aleksovski had committed the crimes that he is accused of. My learned colleague, the Prosecutor, obviously has a different view from the Defence, but the Defence feels that the evidence proceedings have confirmed what Mr. Aleksovski himself had stated in his first appearance before this Tribunal when he stated that he did not consider himself to be guilty on any of the counts from the indictment. The Defence sincerely feels that the proceedings did not confirm the counts of the indictment, and thus the Defence said, in its written statement, that it would like to have an acquittal regarding Mr. Aleksovski. The Defence also considers that there are realistic circumstances in this case to waive the compulsory detention with the provisional release of the accused because the conditions have been met for making such a decision, and it is quite certain that Mr. Aleksovski will respond to any court summons. It is quite certain that the Republic of Croatia will undertake all legal measures in order to support this appearance with its internal legislature, and, of course, there are the circumstances that I talked about. The Defence proposes to Your Honours to consider these exceptional circumstances and proposes that it decides on the provisional release of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Niemann, I think that before giving you the floor, it might be better to hear the representative of the Embassy of Croatia. In that case, we will have the complete position of the Defence. I don't know whether I pronounced your name correctly, Mr. Miljenic. As you have heard, Mr. Mikulicic has presented a series of arguments regarding the cooperation of the Republic of Croatia with the Tribunal so that the Chamber can be sure that should Mr. Aleksovski be provisionally released, he would certainly appear to be tried in this Tribunal. Could you give us the views of the Republic of Croatia regarding the guarantees that the Chamber could have if it were to make such a ruling regarding such a future appearance of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJENIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With your leave, I would like to continue in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We have highly competent interpreters, so please continue in your own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJENIC
utterances.text: In brief, I have been authorised to state that the Republic of Croatia, in the case that Mr. Aleksovski is provisionally released to the territory of the Republic of Croatia of which he is a citizen and is a permanent resident there, will take all legal measures in accordance with its internal laws, especially in accordance with the constitutional law on cooperation with the Tribunal that Mr. Aleksovski performs all the orders of the Court and that he appears before this Tribunal in case he is summoned. Also, I would like to stress that Mr. Aleksovski is one of the examples that the Republic of Croatia has met and will continue to meet the requests of the Tribunal when it arrested him and handed him over to the Tribunal. That is all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Miljenic. For the moment, we have no questions for you, and we can continue our discussion, so please be seated. Mr. Niemann, it is your turn now to give us the views of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please: Your Honours, the position of the Office of the Prosecutor is that we are opposed to the motion by the Defence, and we have provided Your Honours with a written response to the Defence motion. What I now have to say will, in large part, be supplemental to that and also address some of the issues raised by my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic. Your Honours, the import of Rule 65(B) is that release may be ordered by the Trial Chamber only in exceptional circumstances, after hearing the host country, and only if satisfied that the accused will appear for trial, and, finally, if released, that he will not pose any threats to victims, witnesses, or persons. The appearance for trial, Your Honours, is perhaps difficult to understand in the circumstances of this application as the trial has, in large part, been concluded, but clearly the issue is whether he will be here for the rest of the proceedings should he be released. It's upon the accused, Your Honours, to establish that the circumstances are exceptional. In fact, it is an obligation upon them to convince you that he will appear for trial, that he will not pose any danger to victims and witnesses, and, finally, that the host country has been heard. The criteria are conjunctive, so if the accused fails to meet any one of these criteria, then his application must, accordingly, fail. Your Honours, having regard to the seriousness of the offence, the Rules envisage that pre-trial detention will be the rule rather than the exception, and it is only in rare cases - rare cases - where provisional release will be granted. Your Honours, this is not a situation which you have in a domestic jurisdiction where this Court has the power to make an order to the police force of a nation state to keep a person under surveillance, which you can do in a national setting. This is not a situation where the place where the person will reside has the same interest in the Prosecution, as would be in a national setting. In a national setting, the state has an interest in the criminal proceedings going forward and that those criminal proceedings will not be interrupted or frustrated or prevented by the escape or absence of the accused person. So the state itself in a national setting has a vested interest in making sure that that person will attend. When it comes to the deployment of police resources and the taking of measures necessary to secure the attendance of accused persons, in a national setting, the state not only has an interest in making sure that he does attend, but they can deploy their resources and will deploy their resources to see that that happens. That's not the case here. Your Honours have no direct authority to order that borders be checked so that accused persons cannot escape from one jurisdiction to another, so again not like a national setting where airports can be given orders to ensure that persons fitting certain descriptions don't leave or that border points be provided with information. Your Honours are not in that position where you can directly order that. In a national setting, there are various measures that can be put in place to keep the Court alert to the continued presence of the accused when released on bail, and that includes such things as having the accused report regularly to the Court once a week, if necessary, or to an official who is under the direction and control of the Court to ensure that the person is still in the jurisdiction. None of that is available to Your Honours directly, and, Your Honours, we have here, as I've mentioned, no situation where there's a presumption of granting bail. Your Honours, the states involved in the former Yugoslavia where the accused is capable of ending up, some have no interest in this matter, and others are even against the work of the Tribunal. We have no resources to deploy to ensure that he attends for trial. We have no control, as I have said, over borders or over his travel, and we can't do anything to ensure that we check on a regular basis to ensure that he is present within the jurisdiction. This accused did not voluntarily surrender, and the period of time that he spent in The Hague pending trial was not excessive, having regard to the work of the Tribunal and to the complexity of these proceedings. Mr. Mikulicic has gone over the grounds of the Defence in making their motion, and, in summary, I wish to address them as well myself. The first point that he raises, though, relates to no reasonable suspicion that he has committed the crime, and he has said that as part of his motion to be filed before Your Honours. Reasonable suspicion was considered to be a relevant consideration by the Trial Chamber when it dealt with an application for provisional release of an accused person by the name Delalic in the Celebici case, and this was a decision where the Trial Chamber said that the test settled upon was that to have a reasonable suspicion, there must exist facts or information which would satisfy an objective bystander that the accused may have committed the crime. I address this point because it has been specifically raised by Mr. Mikulicic in his motion, and he said that the situation exists here that there is no reasonable suspicion that this accused has committed the crime. Your Honours, in our submission, it is odd to speak of reasonable suspicion at this stage of the proceedings. Normally, this term is used, this "reasonable suspicion," at a much earlier stage of the proceedings. For example, persons are initially interviewed on a reasonable suspicion. Persons are searched on a reasonable suspicion. They are indicted on a reasonable suspicion. They are arraigned on a reasonable suspicion. But they certainly are not convicted on a reasonable suspicion. A suspicion, therefore, is well down the chain of proof. As the case proceeds, the suspicion should move from being a mere suspicion to a prima facie case. In the Tribunal, the prima facie case stage is at the end of the Prosecution case, a point we are well past now; and unlike suspicion, a prima facie case has to be based on evidence, and, Your Honours, it is not necessary for there to be a formal motion that no prima facie case has been established for this to be a relevant consideration in the proceedings. If, at the end of the Prosecution case, it is clear that there has been no prima facie case established, then it is for the Prosecution, firstly, to move to have the counts dismissed. This, in fact, happened in two trials that have proceeded in this Tribunal, the Celebici trial and the Tadic trial. If the Prosecution doesn't do it and the Court is mindful of the fact that there is no prima facie case, it is then for the Tribunal itself, the Trial Chamber itself, to dismiss the counts. Your Honours, if the Prosecution took no action in this case, Your Honours, in our respectful submission, would not have allowed the case to proceed on any counts beyond the Prosecution case if you had come to a firm conclusion that a prima facie case hasn't been established. So, Your Honours, we submit that this case has moved not only beyond reasonable suspicion, it has moved to the point of prima facie case. In our submission, we are at the point of determining whether or not we have proof beyond a reasonable doubt, and the Prosecution would assert that that is the point that we are at and that that has been, in any event, established by the evidence. Your Honours, in our submission, it is inappropriate to raise reasonable suspicion at this level. It is something that has been determined. It was determined when the indictment was submitted by the Prosecutor, it was determined by the confirming Judge, it was determined by Your Honours when you first considered the application for provisional release filed by Mr. Aleksovski in January of this year. It is a matter that was considered by the Prosecution at the end of the presentation of its case and, Your Honours, in our submission, it is not a matter to be raised now as we are past that point. So in respect of that, it is our submission that the Defence assertion that there is no reasonable suspicion has long past. Turning now to the length of the detention. Your Honours, when considering the time spent in custody for the purposes of this particular application, it is our submission that the ten months that Mr. Aleksovski spent in Croatia should not be taken into account. Clearly, Your Honours, if he had come here earlier, the issue of when his trial would have been commenced would have been dealt with much earlier and the case would have clearly been probably over by now without any question. So that first ten months is not a matter that we submit should be taken into account in determining what is an exceptional circumstance. Your Honours, the period of time that he spent pre-trial in The Hague, from when he first arrived in The Hague in April of 1997 to January of 1998, when this trial started, we submit shouldn't be taken into account either, and the reason we say that is because he has already brought an application before you requesting provisional release, and Your Honours have already dealt with that, dealing with the pre-trial period. The period of time that it has taken for his trial, in our submission, is not a matter that should be considered in the process of exceptional circumstances. In our submission, Your Honours, the trial must take its course; it took its course in a manner which was expeditious; there was no party to the proceedings that delayed it or in any way prevented it from going as expeditiously as it can. So it is not appropriate to say in those circumstances that these are exceptional circumstances. If a party to the proceedings could be singled out and be shown to have delayed the proceedings, then perhaps that may be an issue that could be considered by you. But the length of time that a trial takes is a matter in the hands of the Court, and this particular Trial Chamber has been most diligent in ensuring that the proceedings move along as quickly as possible, and it cannot be said that in any way has this been an exceptionally delayed trial, has the process been delayed an exception -- that the process of presenting the evidence before you, both by the Prosecution and Defence, takes time, but that is something which is an inevitable consequence of a trial. There is nothing exceptional about it at all. If there is a large trial and there is lots of evidence on very complicated and difficult issues, this takes time, but it is not exceptional; it is merely a characteristic of the trial, and it is not something that should be raised and presented to you as a basis of why the accused should be given provisional release. So the only matter that, in our submission, is relevant for your consideration is: Is there going to be a delay from now until the conclusion of the trial? Well, Your Honours, this would be a decision made based on speculation. We don't know whether there is going to be a delay. If there is a delay, again, it is a natural incidence or consequence of the trial. It is something that has occurred in the course of the trial. As Mr. Mikulicic hasn't canvassed these issues, I don't have to canvass them either, but we are in a position at the moment where it has been put to you that the trial is definitely going to conclude next June. Well, I don't know how that can be in any way determined, and if it is, and it is because there are difficulties associated with scheduling and so forth which would cause that to happen, then, in my submission, that is not an exceptional circumstance; that is a natural consequence of proceedings which would occur in any jurisdiction where the state is not in a position to immediately make available courts and chambers and so forth to proceed with the trial as expeditiously as one might want. It is not an exceptional circumstance; it is a natural consequence. Now, in our submission, it is quite speculative to say that this case will go that long anyway. We could have a decision tomorrow from the Appeals Chamber, and it could be a decision which could go in any direction, but it could be a decision which could permit the trial to resume immediately, and so that the time lost would be a week or so. We don't know and we simply can't tell that that is going to happen. There is nothing certain about this at all. So this application that is made by the Defence, in our submission, Your Honour, is based on some speculative assumption of something that may or may not occur in the future, and it is not based in any respect on matters that have been dealt with in the past; they have been dealt with and they are not appropriately reconsidered at this stage, in our submission. What, Your Honours, needs to be considered is the consequences, the potential consequences, of granting this accused person provisional release at this stage. Your Honours, the Prosecution has no doubt at all that, if the opportunity presents itself, this accused person will escape the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. The Prosecution has no doubt about that. Why does it have no doubt about it? Because this accused person has seen the full ambit of the Prosecution case against him, he has endeavoured to present his defence, and he knows the strength and the likelihood of his potential conviction. Of course, there is a possibility he may be acquitted, but if he has a choice, if the choice is, "Should I run the risk of being acquitted by going back to The Hague, or should I now take this opportunity to escape?" in our submission, he will take the latter, because it is a natural and normal thing to do in the circumstances. Why could he do it? Because, Your Honours, he is not under the direct control of the Tribunal. Once he leaves The Hague and once he goes back to Croatia, we are then dependant upon what happens in that jurisdiction. Your Honours, it has been said by Mr. Mikulicic and by the representative from the Croatian Embassy that there will be certain measures applied to ensure that Mr. Aleksovski returns to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. These measures are, it seems, apparently to be based on Croatian law. I am not sure that there exists in Croatia a special provision with respect to war crimes, persons charged with war crimes, but it may be that Mr. Mikulicic can assist us with that in terms of pre-trial detention. It may be that there is in existence a more rigid regime singled out for persons charged with those crimes. No doubt, if Mr. Mikulicic is aware of that, he may be able to assist us. Certainly I am no expert in that area. In any event, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber in the Blaskic case, when it came to consider a motion for provisional release, said that the interpretation of the principles applied by this Tribunal should not be influenced by the laws of national states in relation to provisional release, and the view taken by the Trial Chamber in that case was based on the fact that this Tribunal didn't have the resources or facilities at its disposal to enable it to directly enforce its orders. With respect to the enforcement of orders, if Your Honours were to impose certain orders, you would have to be, in our respectful submission, satisfied that they would be carried out. Now, it has been suggested that Mr. Aleksovski was sent here by Croatia as a direct consequence of its desire to ensure that it was a good international citizen and it complied directly with the mandates and requirements of this Tribunal. I wonder, Your Honours, whether that is the case. Certainly from the perspective of the Office of the Prosecutor, it didn't seem to be the case because it was necessary for the Office of the Prosecutor to continually follow up with Croatia on securing Mr. Aleksovski's surrender to this Tribunal. I wonder, Your Honours, what information would become available to you if certain leading members of the International Community, who spoke to and dealt with Croatia on this issue, could be permitted to come forward and give details, if they would do that, of the efforts they put in to securing not only the surrender of Mr. Aleksovski but Mr. Blaskic and Mr. Kordic as well. And I am not sure, Your Honours, that if that material became available, that we would reach the same conclusion that there was prompt and willing action by Croatia in relation to having these accused persons surrendered and whether that willing cooperation would extend to other orders that may be issued in the brief that was filed by the Republic of Croatia in relation to the subpoena of duces tecum argument on the 18th of August, 1997. It is there clearly laid out for Your Honours. It is a public submission clearly laid out how it is asserted by Croatia, in no uncertain terms, that the Tribunal didn't have competence or jurisdiction over states and their officials and it cannot issue compulsory coercive orders to a state or its officials; that the Tribunal does not have the inherent power to order such compulsory coercive orders to states or their officials; the Tribunal does not have the express power to issue such compulsory coercive powers to states or their officials. The limits of the International Tribunal's legal authority and the recognised immunity of states and their officials under international law cannot be circumvented by addressing an order to an individual state official; that the Tribunal lacks competence to determine whether a state has violated its obligations and can neither enforce its orders against states or their officials nor sanction states or their officials for failing to comply with such orders. All such matters must be referred to the Security Council. What does that mean, Your Honours? That means that according to this very state where this person, it has been suggested, should be released provisionally, has maintained previously - and there is no suggestion that it has changed its position, so far as I can see - that you don't have the power to make any orders binding on them in any event. So you can't tell Croatia to provide 24-hour police surveillance. They may or may not do it depending on whether they want to. But their attitude is: You can't do it. You can't tell Croatia to make sure that he doesn't escape and go into another jurisdiction, not according to what their previous position has been, at least, anyway. Perhaps there is an argument that you may be able to order his return to The Hague because, as they tell us, it is part of their constitutional law, but that may not even be enforced either if it is not what they want to do. But the biggest risk, Your Honours, is that he will leave Croatia and that he will go somewhere else. Now, what if he goes back, for example, to the Lasva Valley? He was there during the course of the war. What's going to happen then? We have no one that can go in and do anything about it, and we have no agreement with them to hand him over. So, Your Honours, he could be lost to the jurisdiction at this important stage of the proceedings, and that would indeed be an unfortunate consequence. The victims have come forward and witnesses have come forward and testified under difficult and strenuous conditions. They have an expectation that these proceedings will come to a just conclusion, whatever way Your Honours may decide. These proceedings would be frustrated, they would come to an abrupt and immediate end if this accused didn't return. So, Your Honours, in our submission, if that happened, if that occurred, the very limited resources of the Tribunal, which will only have an opportunity to try the very tip of the iceberg of cases that could potentially be tried in Yugoslavia, would, in this case, have been a nullity; and the consequence of that, Your Honours, is that you would not have been able to contribute to that very important component of the mandate of this Tribunal; namely, contributing to the restoration of peace and security in the former Yugoslavia. If Your Honours would bear with me just a moment? Dealing now, Your Honours, with the question of the accused's state of health. I was given some documents this morning, immediately prior to these proceedings commencing. I haven't had an opportunity to examine them. But up until that point in time, at least I can say, that there was no evidence at all about his state of health. Certainly the Prosecution was not in possession of any information concerning his state of health. Your Honours, if the conditions of his detention are not conducive to maintaining a satisfactory state of health of this accused person, the matter is not resolved by granting him provisional release. The problem is solved, in our respectful submission, by addressing the conditions of detention so as to accommodate his medical condition. This is assuming that there is a genuine problem with his detention conditions which are exacerbating or contributing to his medical condition. It may be, Your Honours, that steps have already been taken. I don't know. I have no information at all to know whether or not special measures are in place or whether or not medical assessments have been made and that the conclusion of those medical assessments is that no special provisions should be put in place. Your Honours, if there is a problem here, then the Prosecution is the first to say that something should be done about it, if that is the case. I very much doubt that it is the case, but if it is, that is our position. In the decision of the Trial Chamber in the case of Kovacevic, Their Honours there said that the accused must establish that he cannot be treated effectively in the Netherlands. It is not a question of whether he cannot be treated effectively in the detention centre, that's in the Netherlands, and they go on to say the fact that "an accused who is ill would be in better spirits and more receptive to medical treatment in his own country with the support of his family does not, in our view, amount to an exceptional circumstance." So, Your Honours, we have no evidence at all about whether or not he can receive appropriate treatment in the Netherlands. There is no evidence at all before us on that. I would be very, very surprised if a modern country, such as the Netherlands, couldn't provide him with the necessary medical support that he needs having regard to his condition, and I would be surprised if Croatia was in a better position than the Netherlands to do that either, frankly. So in my submission, Your Honours, he has the burden to establish to you that he can't receive the treatment here, and in no way has he discharged that burden. We have heard certain assertions made by Mr. Mikulicic from the bar table, but that's not evidence, and there is not much one can do with that. Be that as it may, none of it, so far as I'm not a medical person, and none of it, so far as I know, leads to a conclusion that he cannot be adequately and properly treated here. Your Honours, when coming to consider this application, I think it is necessary, in our submission, for you to have regard to the fact that this is the second time that the application has been made, and in our submission, it would be appropriate for Your Honours to consider carefully whether or not there are any changed circumstances which would justify a provisional release now as opposed to January of 1998, the beginning of this year, when Your Honours came to consider the first motion. If Your Honours conclude that nothing has changed in terms of his circumstances and that they are no more exceptional now than they were before, it is our respectful submission that this motion should be denied. Your Honours, in conclusion, it's our submission that we're dealing with an application here which has been provoked by ultimately something that the accused himself has done. I'm not critical of the course they've taken. It's entirely up to them to decide whether they want to introduce further evidence or not, but the consequence of that was to reopen the case, and they must have expected that the Prosecution would respond, and we did. And if that's what their complaint is about in seeking a justification for this provisional release, then, Your Honours, they can't proceed on the basis that all will ignore their involvement in it and only look to the role that the Prosecution has taken. The Prosecution has its responsibilities and duties, and it responded to a situation it was placed in. If that brought about or will bring about any delay, then that is a reaction to something that the Defence themselves did. In our submission, they can't now come before you and say, "Look at what's happened to us? We've been delayed here by the Prosecution," and to simply ignore the fact that they themselves set upon, embarked upon, the course to introduce this additional material which brought about this delay. In our submission, Your Honours, it's not a matter of simply saying, "The Prosecution is delaying it; therefore, we should be entitled to provisional release." This is a much bigger issue, and, in any event, I emphasise that it is speculative and uncertain as to how long the delay is going to be. There is no reason why some further application can be brought if I'm wrong and it turns out that there is some extensive delay. If that happens, well, that can be done later on down the track when it's established that there has been such a delay. The point is that the trial was not delayed. It proceeded expeditiously. Pre-trial detention was dealt with in the first motion, and, in our submission, the period of time spent in Croatia is not a relevant consideration. If Your Honours will excuse me. Yes, Your Honours, unless there are any other further matters that I can assist you with, those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have anything to add in response or to respond to what Mr. Niemann has said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence would like very briefly to respond to a few points made by my learned friend, Mr. Niemann. So allow me, I will follow the same order in which he presented his views. It is true, as my learned friend Niemann has said, that this Tribunal has no jurisdiction over domestic law when it comes to any coercive measures towards the accused, but it is not true that such jurisdiction doesn't emanate from some other instruments. The Tribunal doesn't have direct jurisdiction because it cannot give orders to domestic police authorities or law enforcement authorities, but the Republic of Croatia is obliged to act in accordance with the requests of the Tribunal pursuant to the constitutional law that it has adopted on cooperation with the Tribunal. Therefore, the jurisdiction of the Tribunal in relation to the local police in Croatia is reflected in the jurisdiction of the competent bodies of the Republic of Croatia which is duty-bound to cooperate with the Tribunal. Without entering into a review of that cooperation in the past, we believe, in this particular case, that that cooperation has been highly effective because it was precisely the Republic of Croatia reacting to the request of the Tribunal that it arrested Aleksovski and surrendered him to the Tribunal. Therefore, the Republic of Croatia has demonstrated its wish to cooperate fully. I think that it is not fair that my learned colleague, Mr. Niemann, should mention as an example of non-cooperation by the Republic of Croatia the subpoena duces tecum from the Blaskic case. I think, pro primo, that this is a case that is still being litigated, so we cannot refer to the arguments of other cases which are still in trial. Secondly, I think that these two cases cannot be compared because, in the other case, the Republic of Croatia feels that those requests affect the security issues of Croatia. It is a well-known fact that the appearance of Mr. Aleksovski in the Tribunal cannot, under any circumstances, be considered a security issue for the Republic of Croatia. Therefore, it is quite realistic to expect that the Republic of Croatia will pro futuro cooperate with the Tribunal as it has already done in surrendering Mr. Aleksovski to the Tribunal. Another question raised by Mr. Niemann is the question of reasonable suspicion for the acts Mr. Aleksovski is being charged with. These are obviously questions of fine shades of meaning in the interpretation. The Defence is fully aware of the degrees of suspicion as proceedings advance, and the Defence did not refer to that level of suspicion that is required for the indictment, nor the prima facie case at the end of the Prosecution case, but the reasonable suspicion that, at the end of the trial, each one of us will think whether the accused has, indeed, committed the offence. So I'm referring to that level of suspicion, rather than the level of suspicion required to initiate a trial in the first place. I do not agree with the Prosecutor that ten months spent in the custody of the Republic of Croatia should not be taken into account. If we view this fact quite pragmatically, it means ten months in detention, and not because Mr. Aleksovski drove a car in a drunken state and killed a pedestrian, but rather because the Republic of Croatia, acting upon orders of this Tribunal, ruled detention for Mr. Aleksovski. Therefore, the time spent by Mr. Aleksovski in detention in the Republic of Croatia should, indeed, be taken into account when ruling on this motion. Colleague Niemann says that by being released Mr. Aleksovski would be in a position to choose to reappear in court or to flee, but there is no such choice before Mr. Aleksovski, because in the event of his provisional release, measures will be enforced against him which will totally deprive him of the possibility of choice, and that is police surveillance and the confiscation of his passport. I think there is no need for me to remind you that there is absolutely no chance of Mr. Aleksovski leaving the territory of the Republic of Croatia if he has no passport and still less his chance of appearing in the Lasva Valley for which, anyway, he has no reason to go because his family is not living there, nor are there any friends there, nor is he employed there. So there is no objective opportunity for him to do that, nor is there any subjective wish on his part to do that. The logic of my learned friend, Mr. Niemann, when speaking about these possibilities and when making comparisons with the subpoena duces tecum hearings is, in the view of the Defence, a logic which is not applicable. It appears as if he is expecting illegal behaviour in advance. In my deep conviction, that cannot be a position taken by a judicial body. The position must be the opposite. One must expect legal behaviour, and illegal behaviour is an exception. In this case, I assure you that the Republic of Croatia will take all the necessary steps to prevent any illegal or unlawful behaviour, and what I have in mind is the possibility of Mr. Aleksovski not appearing in court when called by the Trial Chamber. The question of health: The fact is that Mr. Aleksovski, while being in detention, is aggravating his condition. Here, I agree with Mr. Niemann. I have no doubts regarding the high medical standards applied in the territory of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. What is more, I'm prone to agree with the Prosecutor that those standards are higher than the medical standards in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, perhaps lower than in the Kingdom of Sweden, but that is not the point. The point is not the medical standards. The point is detention in closed space where those standards cannot be applied. I wish to draw your attention to a single illustration. Mr. Aleksovski needs physical therapy on a daily basis. That physical therapy, within the U.N. detention unit, is not provided. It was interrupted, and, according to the situation as it is now, it is applied once in 10 or 15 days which is absolutely inadequate. He needs daily treatment; however, this simply is not possible. Let me repeat that I have no doubts that the Kingdom of the Netherlands can provide this but not under conditions of detention, and here we are dealing with detention. Colleague Niemann has reminded you that the Defence, at the beginning of this year, already submitted a motion for provisional release of the accused, and let me follow on to that by saying that that motion was submitted even before the beginning of trial. In the meantime, evidence has been presented in court, witnesses have been heard, documents have been admitted, maps, videotapes. In the meantime, the health condition of Mr. Aleksovski has deteriorated as a result of detention. Therefore, the conditions today within which we are considering this motion for provisional release are substantially different from the conditions that existed at the beginning of this year when the Trial Chamber received the first motion. Therefore, these two motions cannot, under any circumstances, be identified because they are quite different. Why? Because the circumstances under which they were made are quite different. Therefore, it is our submission that all the circumstances do exist, as we have argued them in writing, and we appeal to this Honourable Trial Chamber to grant the motion for the provisional release of Mr. Aleksovski, with our full assurances that by making such a ruling you would be assisting in improving Mr. Aleksovski's health. You would not, in any sense, undermine these proceedings because the Defence wishes to assure you that Mr. Aleksovski will respond to any summons from this Trial Chamber and appear in The Hague and be ready to face up to your decision, whatever it might be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I see that we have been working for an hour and a half already, but in spite of the need for a break, I would like to address a few questions to Mr. Miljenic and to see whether the Prosecutor or Mr. Mikulicic have any questions, because after that, we can have a break and we can release Mr. Miljenic, because I'm sure he has other things to do. In any event, Mr. Niemann, do you have any questions to address to Mr. Miljenic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, not directly, Your Honour, other than the point that I have made was not to suggest that Croatia would commit any illegality. What I am saying is they have expressed their position in writing in a proceeding which is contrary to the procedures that Your Honours are now examining, which means that if Your Honours are to release him on provisional release, you would be seeking, I would imagine, to support that or back that up with appropriate orders. This state has said in this Chamber in public that it doesn't recognise your authority to do that. Now, unless they have changed their position, our position is that any orders that you do make, one can expect them to be treated in the same way. If there are any questions of Croatia, it is, have they changed their mind since they filed the Blaskic motion? If they have changed their mind, well, that would be interesting. If they haven't changed their mind, then our position remains the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have any questions because it would be preferable to hear those questions while we are together. I have some questions, and after that, perhaps Mr. Miljenic can answer all of those questions together. Do you have any questions, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence has no questions at this time, but if, in the course of further proceedings, there is a need for that, I would like to ask you to permit me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: My question is as follows,

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJENIC
utterances.text: Thank you again for coming and for being here with us. It is true that the Tribunal was established to achieve justice under conditions of peace, which are very difficult conditions, and to make a contribution to peace, but I think these objectives of the Tribunal will never be accomplished unless we establish cooperation among the affected states and the Tribunal, that is, if the persons, I say "the persons" but also the authorities, do not show trust in the Tribunal and the work we are doing here. There is something I would like to ask you. In my opinion, cooperation has to be based on mutual respect and mutual confidence; otherwise, it is not possible to cooperate. My question is as follows: What is the Croatia that you represent here? I'm sorry for using this figure of speech, it is not good or bad, but the Croatia described by the Prosecutor, Mr. Niemann, or the Croatia described by Mr. Mikulicic? Which is the one that you are representing here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJENIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your question. I would first like to state that the Republic of Croatia is not a party in these proceedings, and as you see, I'm not involved in the same way that my colleagues are, but I'm appearing at your request as some sort of friend of the Court in order to help you in reaching your decision. I would like to thank you for your question because it follows upon my desire to comment on the statements by Mr. Mikulicic and Mr. Niemann, as opposed to Mr. Niemann who went into speculation in his remarks regarding the Republic of Croatia. I would just like to state a number of facts that I am able to at this moment, and that is that the Republic of Croatia -- Mr. Mikulicic has warned me to speak a little slower. And that is that the Republic of Croatia, the only two persons who happen to be on its territory and against whom an indictment was raised by this Tribunal, Croatia had arrested them and surrendered them to this Tribunal. This is Mr. Aleksovski and Mr. Skopljak, who was on the same indictment and who was, in the meantime, released in accordance with a decision by the Tribunal. As far as the rest of the accused are concerned who were Croatian citizens, General Blaskic surrendered voluntarily, he had been in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, while in the other cases, the Republic of Croatia intervened in a way in their surrender so that they are all here at the Tribunal. This is as far as the cooperation of the Republic of Croatia is concerned. I would also like to refer to the question of the subpoena which has been raised here in a wrong context, and in my opinion, it was wrongly interpreted. If you permit me, as far as the question of the subpoena, the Prosecution requested for a binding order to be issued to the Republic of Croatia, and in case this was not respected, the Republic of Croatia would be penalised. The Republic of Croatia was opposed to this as something which was contrary to international law, and what the Prosecution forgot to mention, the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal supported the position of the Republic of Croatia, so what was quoted here was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber, and that is that the Tribunal does not have the power to issue orders or penalties against officials or states. So this is a section of international law where Croatia insisted on its rights, just like any other state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, Mr. Miljenic. Could you go more directly to the circumstances surrounding Mr. Aleksovski? What are the guarantees that you can give because Mr. Mikulicic said that the case has still not been completed. So will you please focus on Mr. Aleksovski only?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJENIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to say that this case has been resolved. The Appeals Chamber had made its decision, so this is no longer an issue. As far as Mr. Aleksovski is concerned, I have been authorised to state what I stated at the beginning. I would like to repeat that the Republic of Croatia, in the example of Mr. Aleksovski whom it arrested and in the example of Mr. Skopljak who it also arrested and surrendered to the Tribunal, indicated that so far it has met all the requests of the Tribunal of that kind. The other accused citizens of the Republic of Croatia who are not on Croatian territory could not be arrested. That would be all. If have you have any other questions ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: For the moment, we are satisfied, and we wish to thank you for your cooperation and participation and for coming here and clarifying the situation. You may be seated. We are going to have a break, and you can carry on with your regular duties because we will not need your presence any further. I think it is really time to have a break; otherwise, the interpreters will be really too tired, so let's have a 20-minute break. Then we will have some questions, and then we will have another break to make a determination regarding this motion. A 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I would like to ask

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Mikulicic, that the conditions following the first ruling have changed. Could you elaborate these changes for us, please, with regard to the health of Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I said that, compared to our first request, the circumstances had changed, I thought then at the changed circumstances in regards to two aspects: The first aspect is the health of Mr. Aleksovski and the second one is of a procedural nature. The health of Mr. Aleksovski in relation to the first case early this year has changed because his health difficulties have worsened. I repeat, you yourselves were practically direct witnesses when he collapsed during proceedings at this Tribunal. He was taken to the hospital where he was given medical care. In the meantime, he also had an attack during his stay at the detention unit when he was also taken to the hospital. So these are the circumstances which indicate that his health condition, due to his stay in an enclosed environment, are getting worse. As far as the second point, I had in mind the fact that the evidence procedure had been completed before this Tribunal so you were able to hear testimony from witnesses, and you also could see certain evidence which, in the conviction of the Defence, point to the conclusion that Mr. Aleksovski did not commit those crimes that he is charged with under the indictment. In that sense, I was thinking about the changed circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Another question that I would like to address to Mr. Niemann: After the explanations given by the representative of the Croatian Embassy, have you changed your opinion, or do you maintain your position with regard to the subject of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am reinforced in my position, Your Honour. The position taken by the representative of Croatia was that they have no obligation to comply with orders made by Your Honours and that not only do they not have the obligation to do so, they are content in that position because it has been approved, as they say, by the Appeals Chamber. So my position is now, I submit, much stronger than it was when I made my original submission. May I go on a little bit in relation to that, Your Honour? There was a case before this Tribunal dealing with an accused person called Simic. This accused person was very badly disabled as a consequence of being shot and was in a wheelchair, and he came before the Tribunal and an application was made by him for provisional release, and it is instructive, Your Honours, and it may assist you if I was to just briefly go over the circumstances under which he was given provisional release. He came armed with a letter from the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior of the Republika Srpska. Not only did they offer a monetary sum in relation to his bail, but they undertook in writing under seal that they would comply with any orders issued by the Tribunal, and they specifically spell that out, that they would comply with orders of the Tribunal in relation to the arrest of that accused, if necessary. I think this is in stark contrast to what we have heard in relation to Croatia. There are some other interesting aspects of the order that was given in that case too that may assist Your Honours. There was a letter filed before the Trial Chamber from the International Police Task Force in Bosnia, and in this letter they undertook, on behalf of the Tribunal, to monitor the accused person and to make sure that he complied with conditions that were imposed by the Tribunal. In addition to that, the order was that he would submit himself and go into custody and remain in custody for the length of the trial, so it was purely dealing with pre-trial; it had nothing to do with the trial itself. Once the trial took place, these provisional release conditions would fall away and he would remain in custody until the conclusion of the trial. The next point about it, Your Honours, is that he was severely disabled. This man was in a wheelchair and had been shot in circumstances that had occurred very close to the time that he was arrested and brought here. Under all of these conditions, the Prosecutor agreed. The Prosecutor made no opposition at all to the provisional release and consented to it because there was a reasonable certainty. There wasn't going to be the prospect, which there is here, the very real prospect that we say exists, that there is a trial, all the resources of bringing everyone here for the hearing have all been expended at enormous cost, it can't be repeated again, frankly, because of the limitations on our resources, and in the case of Simic, because he is going to be remanded in custody for the whole period of the trial, there is no risk of that happening, that he will escape at the last moment, and that the trial will amount to naught. That is our very concern here, Your Honours, in relation to that. The issue of the medical condition of the accused that was raised by Mr. Mikulicic a moment ago, Your Honours. We have no evidence of that. All we have are some matters that we may have observed in the course of the proceedings. I have no way of assessing the significance or importance of that in terms of medical assessment. I don't know whether Your Honours are better equipped to do so. But in our submission, if this is a genuine application to seek provisional release based on his medical condition, the very least we should expect to see is for a medical practitioner to come along and to give us details and an explanation as to why his continued detention is incompatible with his medical condition. We have none of that. All we have is we are told that by Mr. Mikulicic. Now, I'm not sure what his medical background is either, but it seems to me that this is the only effective way that this issue can be resolved: We need to have some evidence upon which this order could be based. Your Honours, the last point I would like to make is that it seems to me from what Mr. Mikulicic was saying, that apparently Mr. Aleksovski was receiving adequate medical attention, he was getting his exercises on an appropriate basis at The Hague detention centre, but for some reason or another, that was stopped. I don't know what the basis for that was or why it was stopped or whether it was an appropriate or proper decision to do so. But if there is any question whatsoever that his medical condition is being exacerbated or made worse because of this decision to stop allowing him to have what is necessary for him to do, his exercises or whatever it is, then we strongly urge Your Honours to investigate that matter and see that it is reinstated, because if he needs this sort of assistance, he should get it. We would be the last to be saying that we want anything to happen to him because of some medical condition which could be prevented. We encourage it, and we really do urge Your Honours to investigate that matter. But I say, Your Honours, that this is not a case where provisional release is appropriate and, indeed, to answer Your Honour's original question, I am in no way now assured at all that any orders issued by Your Honours will be complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: To finalise our discussion, which is approaching its close, I should like to give the floor to Mr. Aleksovski to see if he has anything to say or, rather, to add to what Mr. Mikulicic has already said, rather than repeating anything he has said but only if you have any additional remarks to make. Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good day, Your Honours. I took notes about all the things discussed in this Trial Chamber, so I will try briefly to say what I think and also to ask you to permit me to defend myself from freedom. First of all, let's start from the beginning. I addressed this Tribunal and I said that I believe in this Tribunal. It's 12.30, the 2nd of December, '98; I still trust this Tribunal and I will continue to trust this Tribunal. You stated recently, a little ironically, that you like to see me in this courtroom. I understand that that was a little saying, but I would like to tell you that you will have the opportunity to see me again in this Trial Chamber and I believe that I will leave it as an innocent person. Mr. Niemann has just mentioned one of the reasons why I will appear before this Trial Chamber, is that I do not expect objectively to receive a high sentence, strict sentence, and I subjectively expect - I believe this is realistic - that I will leave here as an innocent person, and that's the primary reason why I will come here, in case I am acquitted, in case my motion is granted. My life was always average, normal. Any fear that I will commit any kind of crime or something that is not fitting, as you said in one of the recent sessions, with the behaviour of a regular citizen of the world. It is absurd, in my world view. I don't expect to commit any kind of stupidity. I promise you that. When you said at one of the past sessions that some of my friends and acquaintances would come, you were right. Mrs. Vasvija is my former colleague, and by chance, I know Mr. Tomic because he defended clients who were in my prison. Maybe you didn't know this, but you guessed, let's say. I would also like to say, regarding my motion for provisional release, there are subjective reasons why my counsel and I discussed and proposed for you to permit me to defend myself from liberty. Primarily the reason for this is my health. By chance, life has led me to get some kind of hereditary illnesses. I am not expert in this and I cannot tell you too many details, but I would like to tell you that I have considerable difficulties on account of this, and I will explain what these symptoms are. From '79, the year of '79, I noticed that I have elevated blood pressure, and like any younger man, I was not afraid of illness. I lived normally. I was active in sports. I was, amongst other things, in a local soccer club in Zenica. Also, in the aero club, I was a parachute jumper. But I was advised to stop this, and I did. I continued with my studies, and as you had the opportunity to see, I come from a working class family, wasn't too poor or too rich, I had health insurance in Zenica, I had therapy, with interruptions, but as time went by, these difficulties took their toll. I began to suffer from constant elevated blood pressure. Medical experts would probably explain that better. It went pretty high. I also suffer from tachycardia, which is the faster beating of the heart, and I also suffer from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksovski, excuse me for interrupting you, but we are familiar with your health problems, so there is no need to repeat them. We are familiar with these problems already. So can you please close your statements?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could I say a few more words and then I will conclude?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, but quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to say, Mr. Prosecutor asked the question why I stopped the therapy that I had in the detention unit. First of all, physiotherapy was not stopped because of my will but because of the lack of objective possibilities to implement it the way it is supposed to be because it was senseless to provide therapy in the way possible. The doctor told me that I had problems with my spine, I need to have spinal surgery. The doctor also said I was young, but that this surgery posed considerable threat of paralysis. As far as my heart problems, heart disease, I am on therapy which, because of the kind of therapy, has to be interrupted every four or five months; then I have to take a break and then it begins again because this is very serious therapy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now going to have a break of more or less a half hour, and then we will meet again to render our ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Ruling) (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We are going to render our decision. After having heard the conclusions of the parties, as well as their arguments, and having heard the opinion of the Republic of Croatia, and after having given the floor to the accused, Mr. Aleksovski, the Trial Chamber renders the following decision: The provisional release of an accused cannot be ordered by a Chamber, except under conditions envisaged under Rule 65 and 65(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It is the opinion of the Chamber that the four conditions set out by this Rule are cumulative. It is up to the Defence to prove that each one of those conditions has been fulfilled. The Chamber is of the opinion that, with respect to the motion for the provisional release of Mr. Aleksovski, the Defence has not, in its written motion nor in its oral arguments, given the elements which would have allowed the Judges to reach the conclusion that the conditions of Rule 65(B) have been met and, more specifically, that there were exceptional circumstances regarding the state of health of Mr. Aleksovski. The Judges note, finally, that there are no other exceptional circumstances which lead to the description of the procedure made by the Defence. Consequently, the Trial Chamber rejects the motion for the provisional release of the accused, Mr. Aleksovski. The Trial Chamber requests that the Registry take all useful measures which would allow the accused, Mr. Aleksovski, to have the treatment required by his state of health. That is the decision of the Trial Chamber. The Judges must always act in conformity with the Rules, and the Rules do not allow the Chamber to make any other decision. Therefore, the hearing is adjourned, and the decision has been rendered. Excuse me, but Mr. Olivier Fourmy has drawn my attention to the fact that the decision has been taken in accordance with Article 65(B). In the English transcript, let me say it in English, "... there are no other exceptional circumstances which do not lead to the description ..." Where it says "do not lead to the description," it should read "which arise from the description ..." Is that correct now? Yes. Before adjourning, I should like to address myself to Mr. Aleksovski to say what I have already said. The Rules are the Rules, and the Judges have to implement those Rules, and we are doing that. If we do not meet again before Christmas, I take advantage of this opportunity to wish all of you who do celebrate Christmas a Merry Christmas.
